en: The *Kṣemapradīpa-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
There was a great assembly of twenty thousand bhikṣus,
together with many bodhisattvas, namely the great bodhisattva assembly including Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī, and others.

At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his alms bowl; accompanied by Maitreya Bodhisattva, he entered the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for food, eventually arriving at the palace of King Bimbisāra, whereupon he wished to enter.

At that time, King Bimbisāra’s queen, Khemāvatī, was seen upon a multi-storied pavilion. Upon seeing the World-Honored One, her mind became even more pure; she descended from the pavilion, spread out a highly precious cloth named *pāṭuṇa*, and the Tathāgata sat upon it, while Maitreya Bodhisattva sat upon a *niṣīdana*.

At that time, after the World-Honored One and Maitreya Bodhisattva had both taken their seats, the King’s consort, Kṣamāvatī, adorned her body with every kind of ornament. She prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and likewise paid homage to Maitreya Bodhisattva. Then, before the World-Honored One, she composed her countenance and sat upright; with a heart full of reverence, she desired to hear the Dharma being preached.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing Queen Kṣemavatī with her body fully adorned with all manner of ornaments, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings and bringing great profit to all living beings, knowing [the answer] yet asked intentionally of Queen Kṣemavatī: "Kṣemavatī!"
"What is the name of that tree?
Your body is now adorned with such-colored fruit, possessing a supreme radiance, exquisite and wonderful.
Then, the King’s consort, Khemāvatī, replied in verse:
“The foremost of great men, knowing [the answer], nevertheless asked me:
‘What is the name of that tree?
Upon it you have hung such fruits.’”
That tree is named Puṇya; I planted it in a former life.
This fruit is its fruit, which I now eat in this manner.
Furthermore, having already planted that tree for the Śrāvakas of the Perfectly Awakened One, [I have attained this result].
Abiding on the path to enlightenment, one seeks the ground of perfect awakening.
Moistened by the water of generosity and ethical discipline, that tree grows;
once that tree has grown, it produces this sublime fruit.
The powers of patience and diligence can cause that tree to grow;
once that tree has grown, it produces this stainless fruit.
The blossoming flowers of meditative concentration and wisdom make that tree magnificent and sublime.
I now eat this fruit, as the World-Honored One has seen it.
Like the fruits of a forest tree and the like, all depend upon the mountain;
while the branches and leaves grow, they remain unmoved above and below.
Thus that great tree was planted by me in a previous life through my roots of goodness;
it benefits all sentient beings so that they may attain the Buddha-dharma.
Of such a tree of merit, this [present life] of mine is but its flower.
I shall eat this meal for now; the fruit still remains behind.
As for the fruit of supreme enlightenment, the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Buddha—having cast off this inferior female body, I shall surely attain that fruit hereafter.
I shall become a true man, the most supreme among all beings;
having reached the further shore of all dharmas, I shall possess the all-encompassing vision of omniscience.
I shall liberate all sentient beings from all suffering and fear.
"All shall return to me; I have compassion for all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the King’s wife, Khemā, saying these words:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, Kṣamāvatī!

You are able to benefit so many people, bring peace and happiness to so many people, have compassion for the world, and provide benefit, peace, and happiness to the entire assembly of devas and humans.
At that time, the King’s consort, Khemāvatī, having heard the Buddha’s praise, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By what causes and conditions do these thirty-two marks of a Great Man and eighty minor characteristics of this body result in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge?”

Furthermore, from what do the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity—such various, immeasurable, incomparable, and unspeakably infinite, innumerable Buddha-dharmas—as well as all others arise?
When the King’s consort, Kṣamāvatī, had thus questioned him, the Buddha spoke these verses:
“I, too, was just like this; In past lives I planted that tree For the benefit of sentient beings, Seeking the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.”
Cultivating generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, And the accumulation of diligence, meditative concentration, and harmony;
Furthermore, at all times, Constantly practicing meditative concentration and wisdom;
Toward all sentient beings, Never giving rise to an evil mind.
By constantly practicing an impartial mind, one attains Buddhahood today.
Always remaining equal toward the beloved and the unloved, as well as toward virtuous friends and enemies,
once this impartial mind is attained, the tree of merit grows.
This great tree of my body gathers immeasurable merit;
it was once a wheel-turning king, also served as King Śakra,
and further acted as a Great Brahmā King, possessing manifold wealth and joy.
"The inconceivable Buddha-dharma, whose characteristics are now likewise attained.
At that time, the king’s consort, Kṣamāvatī, having heard this exposition of such merits, praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
“I feel the utmost joy in accordance with the words of the Blessed One.
He then addressed the Tathāgata in verse:
“As the most excellent among superior men, Thus shall I train in accordance [with your teaching].”
Just as he originally trained and trained well, [becoming] an ocean of boundless merit;
now I train in the training of the Buddha, reaching the further shore of all merits.
May I leave behind the suffering of birth and death, and attain such a state as that of the Muni.
In all my previous places of birth, I have practiced the giving of alms;
by virtue of all that merit, may I attain the peerless wisdom of a Buddha.
In all my past and present births, I have maintained the observance of the precepts.
May all that merit lead them to attain the wisdom of a Tathāgata;
may my cultivation of patience, diligence, samādhi, prajñā, and so forth—
may all such things as these bring about the complete accomplishment of the Buddha-dharma.
Through all the wholesome deeds practiced by my body, speech, and mind,
may I attain great enlightenment and seek the merit of the Buddha’s wisdom.
May I cast off this female form and obtain the superior body of a man.
Having attained the body of a great man, one successively attains the Buddha-body.
Having attained supreme enlightenment, one turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma,
liberating sentient beings bound within the prison of birth and death.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to the king’s wife, Khemāvatī, saying:
“Excellent! These words you have spoken—excellent!”
"With a virtuous mind and aspiration, you shall destroy Māra and attain perfect enlightenment.

When the King’s consort, Kṣemavatī, had received this personal prophecy from the World-Honored One, she was filled with joy; giving rise to a supreme and exalted mind and a resolute intention, she offered the World-Honored One abundant quantities of *khādaniya* (solid food), *bhojaniya* (soft food), and *svādaniya* (delicious food), providing every necessity in full measure, and likewise made offerings of food to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal, set aside his bowl and washed his hands.
Having washed his hands, he further preached the Dharma for the royal consort Khemā, instructing, teaching, exhorting, and guiding her until she was filled with joy.
Then he bestowed upon her this prediction: "Khemā!..."

In the future, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood, to be known by the name Guṇaratnavijaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Your Buddha-world is the foremost in purity; it is free from the miseries of the evil realms, and its mind is joyful and delighted, adorned with exquisite wonders—the supreme, pure dwelling place of bodhisattvas.
"You shall attain such a world as this, adorned and purified by the Buddha.
When the Buddha spoke this Dharma-gate, many thousands of upāsakas all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
and many thousands of beings among humans, devas, and the world attained a mind of compliance, free from doubt regarding the Dharma.

When the Tathāgata had finished speaking, Kṣamāvatī, Maitreya Bodhisattva, the entire assembly, as well as the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the World-Honored One said, were all greatly rejoiced.
The Sutra on the Prediction of Kṣemapati’s Attainment of Buddhahood
